title: When seva feeds the ego
hookLine: serving to be seen feeds the very ego seva is meant to thin
last: SEVA OF THE MIND — GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.

cards: Saturday morning, serving food at a shelter. Good work, and a tired, happy walk home. Then a tiny voice asks: should I post about it?
Just one picture. Not to brag. Just so people know.
Or it's quieter than that. All the dishes at a family dinner, washed, and a small wait for someone to notice. Nobody does, and it stings.
That sting is worth a look. It isn't the mark of a bad person. The Gurus wrote about it again and again, and today it gets a name.

teach.b: Haumai. Hau means I. Mai means me.

I, me. It's the Gurus' word for ego: the self that puts itself at the center of everything, that wants credit, that keeps count. In Sikh teaching, haumai is the main thing that stands between a person and God.
Not some outside enemy. The inside one. Here's the trap this week has been building toward.
Seva is meant to thin haumai: you serve, you forget yourself, the I gets a little smaller.

teach.h: SEVA TO BE SEEN FEEDS THE I.
teach.b: But serve in order to be seen, and the seva itself becomes food for the ego. The more you do, the bigger it gets. Same dishes, same shoes, opposite result.
That's why the Gurus keep stressing nishkam, without wanting. Now the hopeful part. Guru Angad has a line in the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: THE MEDICINE IS WITHIN IT TOO.
teach.b: In paraphrase: haumai is a long, deep illness, but the medicine is within it too. The place the sickness lives is where the cure can start. Noticing yourself wanting credit is already the medicine working.
And Guru Nanak says in the Japji that someone who understands the divine order, the hukam, stops saying I. So the practice isn't to beat yourself up for wanting to be seen. That's just more I.

teach.h: NOTICE IT, SMILE, LET IT GO.
teach.b: Notice it, smile at it, and let it go, the way you'd smile at a child who wants you to watch them jump.
Then do the next bit of service anyway.

how: Sikh teaching names haumai, ego, as the root obstacle between a person and God, and Sikhs are taught to do seva humbly and without seeking recognition so that it thins the ego rather than feeding it.

o: a short prayer said before a meal
the soul, the part of you that lives on after death
the ego, the self that wants credit and keeps count

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: wanting credit means your seva doesn't count
the Gurus say to notice it and let it go; noticing is already the medicine working.
hau is I, mai is me: the self at the center.
in Sikh teaching the main obstacle to God is an outside enemy

games.q: you've just done a big day of seva, and you catch yourself drafting a post about it. what does the teaching on haumai suggest?
o: feel ashamed and stop doing seva.
notice the wanting, smile at it, and let it go.
post it; the good work is what matters.
games.why: the Gurus say haumai holds its own cure. noticing it without beating yourself up is the practice; then you serve again.

practice: Think back over the last few days of seva, the unseen kindness, the shoes, the dish, the tenth, the thing you taught, and find a moment you wanted someone to know.
Don't judge it; just see it clearly, like spotting a cat on a windowsill: oh, there you are. Smile at it, and let it go.

wordCard.voice: Haumai. I, me: the ego that wants credit, which seva is meant to thin, and which the Gurus say holds its own cure.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: I, me; the ego.

carryVoice: Your line: serve, then forget it. Wanting credit is human, and noticing it is the medicine. That's day one hundred two.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Angad: haumai is a deep illness, but its medicine is within it)
Japji Sahib, stanza 2, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (one who understands the hukam does not speak in ego)
